The hall smelled of tallow, old paper and oiled leather. A woman behind the counter — thick-armed, gray streaking her braid, a quill tucked behind one ear — looked up from a ledger and took his hand in a grip that had shaken a hundred like it. "Alaric Red. Fresh face, that's plain enough." She let go and set the ledger aside. "Registration, then. Two silver, one-time, and it puts you on the rolls at Novice rank. That's the Guild's rank — starts at Novice, tops out at Legend. It's what jobs you're allowed to take and how the Guild trusts you. Nothing to do with how strong you actually are; that's your Power Rank, and we measure it, we don't grant it. Yours is F right now, if you're wondering, same as every new blood that walks in." She pulled a slotted wooden tray from under the counter and turned it toward him. Beside it sat a smooth gray stone about the length of a hand, worn glassy at one end. "You pay the two silver, I take your details — name, age, what you can do, that sort of thing — and you lay your palm on the measuring stone. It reads your Level and your Power and we write it down plain. Then you get your slip and the boards are open to you." She nodded past his shoulder, toward the papered boards near the door, where a few slips fluttered in the draft from the open doors. "So. Two silver, whenever you're ready."

mes:
The hall smelled of tallow, old paper and oiled leather. A woman behind the counter — thick-armed, gray streaking her braid, a quill tucked behind one ear — looked up from a ledger and took his hand in a grip that had shaken a hundred like it.

"Alaric Red. Fresh face, that's plain enough." She let go and set the ledger aside. "Registration, then. Two silver, one-time, and it puts you on the rolls at Novice rank. That's the Guild's rank — starts at Novice, tops out at Legend. It's what jobs you're allowed to take and how the Guild trusts you. Nothing to do with how strong you actually are; that's your Power Rank, and we measure it, we don't grant it. Yours is F right now, if you're wondering, same as every new blood that walks in."

She pulled a slotted wooden tray from under the counter and turned it toward him. Beside it sat a smooth gray stone about the length of a hand, worn glassy at one end.

"You pay the two silver, I take your details — name, age, what you can do, that sort of thing — and you lay your palm on the measuring stone. It reads your Level and your Power and we write it down plain. Then you get your slip and the boards are open to you."

She nodded past his shoulder, toward the papered boards near the door, where a few slips fluttered in the draft from the open doors.

"So. Two silver, whenever you're ready."

Don't lose it; it's your proof of standing and replacing it costs you. Board's by the door, jobs posted as they come in. He pulled the slip from its pin and carried it to the counter. The clerk read it upside down as he laid it down, and something in her face shifted — not alarm, just arithmetic. "Mossback Warrens." She took the slip, checked the seal, and opened the ledger to a fresh line. "Solo, on your first day." It wasn't quite a question. The quill started moving anyway, recording his name against the contract. "Level One's the shallow floor. Goblin scouts and warriors, by the last reports. The Guild doesn't tell Novices what they can and can't take, but I'll tell you what the slip doesn't: folk who come back down those stairs usually come back the same way they went up, quick. The ones who linger are the ones we send people after." She stamped the slip, blew on the ink, and held it out. The Guild seal sat at the bottom in red wax, plain and unmarked. "That's your contract. Bring it back when the floor's cleared and the seal goes READY — that's when you get paid. A hundred and fifty coppers." She pushed the ledger aside and looked at him properly for the first time. "Warrens are east, off the old quarry track. Half a day's walk, the moss-grown hill — you'll see it before you see anything else. Water's pooled in the low ground around it, so mind your footing." She took up the next paper in her stack, then paused. "Staff's good for goblins in the open. Down in those tunnels, everything's close. That's all I'll say about it."

He pulled the slip from its pin and carried it to the counter. The clerk read it upside down as he laid it down, and something in her face shifted — not alarm, just arithmetic.

"Mossback Warrens." She took the slip, checked the seal, and opened the ledger to a fresh line. "Solo, on your first day." It wasn't quite a question. The quill started moving anyway, recording his name against the contract. "Level One's the shallow floor. Goblin scouts and warriors, by the last reports. The Guild doesn't tell Novices what they can and can't take, but I'll tell you what the slip doesn't: folk who come back down those stairs usually come back the same way they went up, quick. The ones who linger are the ones we send people after."

She stamped the slip, blew on the ink, and held it out. The Guild seal sat at the bottom in red wax, plain and unmarked.

"That's your contract. Bring it back when the floor's cleared and the seal goes READY — that's when you get paid. A hundred and fifty coppers." She pushed the ledger aside and looked at him properly for the first time. "Warrens are east, off the old quarry track. Half a day's walk, the moss-grown hill — you'll see it before you see anything else. Water's pooled in the low ground around it, so mind your footing."

She took up the next paper in her stack, then paused. "Staff's good for goblins in the open. Down in those tunnels, everything's close. That's all I'll say about it."
